title: Time and daily actions
japaneseTitle: みんなの日本語 第4課
summary: Say when things happen, distinguish calendar dates from durations, define time ranges, and move polite verbs between non-past and past.
sourceFiles: みんなの日本語　第4課.pdf
takeaways: Exact clock times take に; relative times usually do not.
から and まで independently mark the start and end of a range.
ました and ませんでした place an action in the past.

grammar.title: Time expressions: when to use に
grammar.pattern: Exact time + に / relative time without に
grammar.summary: Use に to pin an action to an exact clock time or calendar point. Relative expressions such as [[来週|らいしゅう]] and [[毎日|まいにち]] normally stand without it.
grammar.detail: A weekday can take に when you present it as a scheduled day: [[金曜日|きんようび]]に働きます. With a time range, attach から and まで directly to the clock times instead.

examples.english: I go to bed at 8 PM.
I will study Japanese next week.

tokens.gloss: day-point marker; optional in some contexts

examples.note: Weekdays may take に or omit it; に makes the day feel like a scheduled point.

grammar.caution: Do not add に after relative time words such as [[今日|きょう]], [[明日|あした]], [[昨日|きのう]], [[毎日|まいにち]], or [[来週|らいしゅう]] in basic time expressions.

grammar.title: Calendar dates, durations, and day order
grammar.pattern: Date: N[[日|にち]] / duration: N[[日間|にちかん]] / sequence: N[[日目|にちめ]]
grammar.summary: Use the calendar-date reading for a day of the month. Add [[間|かん]] to say how long something lasts, and add [[目|め]] to say which day in a sequence it is.
grammar.detail: Context can make a form such as [[２日|ふつか]] mean either the 2nd day of the month or two days. Among these day-number readings, day 1 is the only base-reading exception: [[１日|ついたち]] is the 1st of the month, while [[１日|いちにち]] means one day. From day 2 onward, the base reading is generally the same for the date and the number of days; add [[間|かん]] to make a duration explicit, as in [[２日間|ふつかかん]] or [[１日間|いちにちかん]]. For the third day in a sequence, use [[３日目|みっかめ]].

examples.english: I will go to Tokyo on May 3.
I went to school for two days.
The exam was on the third day.

grammar.caution: Do not treat [[１日|ついたち]] and [[１日|いちにち]] as interchangeable: the first is the 1st day of the month, while the second means one day. [[間|かん]] marks a duration; [[目|め]] marks order in a sequence.

grammar.title: Month names: がつ or げつ?
grammar.pattern: Number + がつ / calendar compound + げつ
grammar.summary: Use がつ after a number to name a month. Use げつ in calendar compounds such as [[月曜日|げつようび]], [[今月|こんげつ]], and [[来月|らいげつ]].
grammar.detail: The same character 月 changes reading according to the word. Numbered months use がつ: [[五月|ごがつ]]. Compound words for a month or weekday commonly use げつ: [[今月|こんげつ]] and [[月曜日|げつようび]].
grammar.caution: Do not use げつ for a numbered month: [[五月|ごがつ]] is May, not ごげつ. Do not use がつ in [[月曜日|げつようび]].

grammar.title: Place: choose に or で by role
grammar.pattern: [[場所|ばしょ]] に [[行きます|いきます]] / [[場所|ばしょ]] に あります / [[場所|ばしょ]] で Verb
grammar.summary: For a place, に marks a destination or where something exists. で marks where an action happens.
grammar.detail: Choose the particle from the place's role, not from the English word “at.” Movement goes toward a destination, existence stays at a location, and an action unfolds in a setting.

examples.english: There is a book on the desk.

grammar.caution: [[東京|とうきょう]]に[[行きます|いきます]] means movement to Tokyo; [[東京|とうきょう]]で[[働きます|はたらきます]] means working in Tokyo.

grammar.title: [[始まる|はじまる]] vs [[始める|はじめる]]: what starts and who starts it
grammar.pattern: Thing が [[始まります|はじまります]] / person が thing を [[始めます|はじめます]]
grammar.summary: Use [[始まる|はじまる]] when something starts by itself or the sentence focuses on the event. Use [[始める|はじめる]] when someone actively starts something.
grammar.detail: The thing that starts is marked with が: [[授業|じゅぎょう]]が[[始まります|はじまります]]. The thing being started is marked with を: [[私|わたし]]は[[勉強|べんきょう]]を[[始めます|はじめます]]. The first verb is intransitive; the second is transitive.
grammar.caution: Do not interchange the particles: [[授業|じゅぎょう]]が[[始まります|はじまります]] describes the class starting, while [[先生|せんせい]]が[[授業|じゅぎょう]]を[[始めます|はじめます]] describes the teacher starting it.

grammar.title: Pin an action to a time
grammar.summary: Use に with exact points such as clock times and calendar dates.

examples.english: I wake up at seven thirty every morning.

examples.note: Weekdays may use に or omit it.

grammar.caution: [[今日|きょう]], [[明日|あした]], [[昨日|きのう]], [[毎日|まいにち]], [[今朝|けさ]] and similar relative times normally omit に.

grammar.title: Draw a time span
grammar.pattern: Time から Time まで
grammar.summary: から marks the starting boundary and まで marks the ending boundary. Either can stand alone.

examples.english: I work from nine until five.
The lunch break is until one.

grammar.title: Ask and answer about the past
grammar.summary: Use ました for an affirmative past action and ませんでした for a negative past action.

tokens.reading: べんきょうしませんでした

recall.prompt: Does [[毎朝|まいあさ]] take に?
recall.answer: Normally no. Relative/repeating time words do not need に.

recall.prompt: What marks the end of a time range?
Make [[働きます|はたらきます]] past-negative.
recall.answer: [[働きませんでした|はたらきませんでした]]

recall.prompt: How do you read 月 in [[五月|ごがつ]] and [[月曜日|げつようび]]?
recall.answer: がつ in 五月; げつ in 月曜日.

recall.prompt: How do you distinguish the 3rd day, three days, and the third day in a sequence?
recall.answer: [[３日|みっか]] can mean the 3rd day or three days by context; [[３日間|みっかかん]] makes the duration explicit; [[３日目|みっかめ]] means the third day in a sequence.
